Tesla Turned Cars Into Phones. Now They Keep Crashing

Hook

Top hooks, yt-script score

Look and device

Running device

Running 'EYES OFF ROAD' meter in the top-left corner: metres driven blind per task, ticking up whenever a screen is touched. Recurring symbol: Dave's nodding-dog dashboard toy, which nods happily at buttons and shakes its head at screens.

Look

Consumer-tech rant explainer in the house 2D style (Gumball/t-shirt rig), painterly plates: a rainy M62 motorway at dusk seen through a windscreen, a 2005 estate-car dashboard full of chunky buttons, a modern glowing tablet dashboard, a Swedish test track, a car-design studio, a German boardroom, a glossy motor-show stand, a monthly-bill kitchen table, a scrapyard, a Rome launch stage, a Porsche-style workshop. Cold open

1:04 · 5 shots · 161 words
  1. 0.01WIDE11.7s

    April 2019. Key Largo, Florida. Just after nine at night, a Tesla Model S is cruising on Autopilot. The driver drops his phone, and reaches down to find it.

    Night two-lane road through mangroves, a dark saloon glides along with Autopilot glow on the dash; inside, a phone slips off the seat and the driver bends down.

    KEY LARGO · APRIL 2019

    ANIMATIONPhone slides off the seat; driver's head dips below the window line.

  2. 0.02MED12.8s

    The road ends at a T-junction. The car doesn't stop. At over sixty miles an hour, it runs straight through and hits a parked SUV. A young couple are standing beside it.

    Stop sign and flashing warning light rush past; impact shown as a white flash and debris from a distance (no gore); the parked SUV spins; sirens' blue light.

    ANIMATIONWarning lights flash past, white flash, debris, cut to blue lights.

  3. 0.03MED15.8s

    Twenty-two-year-old Naibel Benavides was killed. Her boyfriend was badly hurt. In 2025, a jury in Miami decided the driver was mostly to blame, but that Tesla was one third responsible too. The bill: around two hundred and forty-three million dollars.

    Courtroom: jury box silhouettes, a memorial candle and photo frame (no likeness), a verdict card '1/3 TESLA' and a counter to $243M.

    JURY: TESLA 1/3 RESPONSIBLE · ~$243M

    ANIMATIONVerdict card stamps; counter rolls; candle flickers.

  4. 0.04MED16.6s

    Here's the strange bit. Holding your phone at the wheel in Britain can cost you six points and a two-hundred-pound fine. But a carmaker bolting a fifteen-inch tablet to your dashboard, and telling you the car can drive itself? Apparently that's fine.

    Split: a UK police officer writes a ticket for a phone; on the right a salesman proudly unveils a giant screen in a showroom; nodding dog shakes its head.

    6 POINTS + £200

    ANIMATIONTicket rips off the pad; the screen unveiling gets sparkles.

  5. 0.05TITLE7.5s

    So did Tesla turn the car into a phone? And is that why some of them keep crashing?

    Title card: a car dashboard morphing into a giant phone, with a home bar where the speedo was; a crack runs across it.

    YOUR CAR IS A PHONE NOW

    ANIMATIONDashboard melts into a phone; title stamps; crack.

How the tablet ate the dashboard

1:03 · 5 shots · 156 words
  1. 1.01WIDE12.1s

    So how did we get here? Rewind to 2012. Tesla launches the Model S with a seventeen-inch touchscreen in the middle of the dash, and the world loses its mind.

    A bright launch stage in 2012; a sleek saloon rolls out; the giant portrait screen glows; a crowd of phones film it.

    2012 · TESLA MODEL S

    ANIMATIONCar rolls in, screen powers on with a glow, flashbulbs pop.

  2. 1.02MED7.2s

    The logic sounded clever. Phones got better when they lost their buttons. So surely cars would too?

    A chunky old mobile with keypad buttons melts into a sleek smartphone; arrow points to a button-covered dashboard melting into a tablet.

    PHONE LOGIC

    ANIMATIONButtons pop off and fly away like popcorn.

  3. 1.03MED12.1s

    And every new model came with more features. Massage seats, ambient lighting, twelve drive modes. There simply wasn't room for a button for everything, so the screen swallowed the lot.

    Engineers in a design studio pile labelled toggles (MASSAGE, AMBIENT, DRIVE MODE) onto a crowded dashboard until it overflows; the screen opens like a mouth and gulps them.

    ANIMATIONButtons stack, wobble, then get sucked into the screen.

  4. 1.04CU13.9s

    But there's one big problem. A button you can feel. A screen you have to look at. And at seventy miles an hour, there's only one thing your eyes should be looking at. The road.

    Close-up on Dave's eyes flicking down to the glow, then up to the road; the windscreen view drifts towards the hard shoulder.

    EYES ON THE ROAD

    ANIMATIONEye-line arrow flicks down/up; road view drifts; rumble strip buzz.

  5. 1.05MED17.3s

    And when the screen dies, things you need die with it. In 2021, Tesla recalled about a hundred and thirty-five thousand Model S and Model X cars because the screen's memory chip could wear out, taking the demister and the reversing camera with it.

    Old Tesla-style saloon dash: the big screen flickers and goes black; the windscreen fogs over; a reversing-camera icon fades; recall notice slaps on: 135,000 CARS.

    RECALL 2021: ~135,000 CARS

    ANIMATIONScreen glitches to black; fog creeps; recall stamp.

The 70 mph test

1:12 · 7 shots · 178 words
  1. 2.01WIDE7.2s

    In 2022, a Swedish car magazine called Vi Bilägare decided to measure exactly how bad this is.

    A Swedish test airfield at dawn, pine trees, a line of twelve cars on the runway, a man with a stopwatch and clipboard.

    VI BILÄGARE · 2022

    ANIMATIONCars roll into a line; stopwatch glints.

  2. 2.02MED13.2s

    They took twelve cars, drove each one at about seventy miles an hour, and gave the driver four simple jobs. Change the radio, adjust the heating, reset the trip computer, dim the dashboard.

    Checklist card with four ticks; a driver in a helmet runs through each task as the car speeds down the runway.

    4 SIMPLE TASKS

    ANIMATIONChecklist items tick off one by one.

  3. 2.03MED9.8s

    The winner? A 2005 Volvo V70. Seventeen years old, covered in buttons. All four jobs in ten seconds, about three hundred metres of road.

    An old boxy estate on a podium with a winner's rosette; counter: 10 SECONDS · 306 m; nodding dog nods.

    2005 VOLVO V70: 10 s · 306 m

    ANIMATIONPodium rises, rosette pins on, counter counts up fast.

  4. 2.04MED9.8s

    The slowest was the MG Marvel R, an all-screen electric SUV. Forty-five seconds. Nearly one and a half kilometres of road, driven half blind.

    A shiny screen-filled SUV; the EYES OFF ROAD meter spins up past 1,400 m; behind it a scale of football pitches laying out end to end.

    MG MARVEL R: 44.9 s · ~1.4 km

    ANIMATIONMeter spins; pitch strips unroll across the frame.

  5. 2.05MED11.7s

    And it gets sillier. In some Teslas, the glovebox opens from a menu on the screen. Even the gears moved there. Swipe up for drive, swipe down for reverse.

    Dave in a white saloon tapping the screen to open the glovebox; a gear slider on screen; he swipes the wrong way and the car lurches backwards into a bin.

    GLOVEBOX: SCREEN MENU

    ANIMATIONSwipe gesture, car jolts back, bin wobbles.

  6. 2.06MED9.8s

    Then Volkswagen tried to out-minimal Tesla. It replaced real buttons, even on the steering wheel, with touch-sensitive pads that you could brush by accident.

    A German design studio; a designer peels real buttons off a steering wheel and replaces them with shiny touch pads; a driver's thumb brushes one and the volume blasts.

    ANIMATIONButtons peeled off; accidental brush triggers a volume blast.

  7. 2.07MED10.9s

    Owners hated it. And in 2025 VW's design boss, Andreas Mindt, said physical buttons were coming back, and promised they would never, ever make that mistake again.

    Angry owners with placards; VW design boss at a press conference with a quote card; a box of buttons gets carried back into the studio.

    "NEVER, EVER" · ANDREAS MINDT, VW

    ANIMATIONQuote card slams; buttons marched back in.

Autopilot: the name problem

1:14 · 5 shots · 187 words
  1. 3.01WIDE14.7s

    Then there's the name. Autopilot. To most people, that sounds like a plane that flies itself. In reality, it's a driver-assist system. You're meant to keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel.

    Airliner cockpit cartoon with a pilot reading a newspaper, then wipe to a Tesla cabin with the word AUTOPILOT glowing; small print zooms in: 'hands on wheel, eyes on road'.

    "AUTOPILOT" = DRIVER ASSIST

    ANIMATIONPlane wipes to car; small print magnifies.

  2. 3.02MED15.1s

    America's road-safety regulator, NHTSA, spent about three years looking at nine hundred and fifty-six crashes. It found Tesla's system for checking drivers were paying attention was weak, and linked it to crashes that killed at least thirteen people.

    US safety agency office: investigators with folders, a wall of crash pins on a US map, a stamp 'WEAK DRIVER ENGAGEMENT', counter to 956 and 13.

    NHTSA: 956 CRASHES REVIEWED · 13 FATAL

    ANIMATIONPins drop on the map; stamp lands.

  3. 3.03MED14.3s

    In December 2023, Tesla recalled more than two million cars, nearly every one it had sold in America, to update the software. The fix? More warnings. Delivered, of course, over the air. Like a phone update.

    A car park of identical white saloons; each screen shows a download progress bar; a little 'UPDATE INSTALLED' tick; nodding dog shakes its head.

    RECALL: 2,000,000+ CARS (DEC 2023)

    ANIMATIONProgress bars fill in sync; ticks pop.

  4. 3.04MED15.8s

    Then California stepped in. In December 2025, a judge ruled that Tesla's Autopilot and Full Self-Driving marketing had been misleading. Tesla stopped using the word Autopilot in the state, and dropped Autopilot as a product in the US and Canada.

    California DMV building, a judge's ruling card 'MISLEADING'; a sign painter scrapes the word AUTOPILOT off a showroom window.

    CALIFORNIA DMV: MARKETING MISLEADING

    ANIMATIONRuling slams; letters scraped off one by one.

  5. 3.05MED14.3s

    And the questions haven't stopped. In 2026, the regulator stepped up its investigation into Full Self-Driving to cover more than three million Teslas, after reports of cars running red lights and drifting into the wrong lane.

    Junction at dusk: a red light, a car rolling through it; an investigator's magnifying glass; counter 3,200,000; 'ENGINEERING ANALYSIS' badge.

    NHTSA FSD PROBE: ~3.2M CARS

    ANIMATIONLight turns red, car rolls through, magnifier sweeps.

When the doors won't open

1:11 · 5 shots · 178 words
  1. 4.01WIDE14.3s

    But the scariest part isn't the screen. It's the doors. Most Teslas don't open with a simple lever and a cable. They open with a button, powered by electricity. A phone, basically, with a door attached.

    Close-up cutaway of a car door: an old car's metal cable and lever on the left; on the right a Tesla-style door with a glowing button, wires and a little battery.

    ANIMATIONCable pulls the latch on the left; button blips on the right.

  2. 4.02MED16.9s

    After a bad crash, that electric power can fail. There are manual releases inside, but they're often hidden, unlabelled, and hard to find in a panic. Bloomberg found at least fifteen deaths where people couldn't get a Tesla door open after a crash.

    Dark cabin after a crash: dash lights die; a hand presses a dead door button; a torch beam searches the door pocket for a hidden pull tab; Bloomberg tag; counter 15.

    BLOOMBERG: AT LEAST 15 DEATHS

    ANIMATIONLights flicker out; torch searches; tab revealed.

  3. 4.03MED13.9s

    In November 2024, a Cybertruck crashed and caught fire in Piedmont, California. Three students died. Police said speed and impairment caused the crash. But their families are suing Tesla, claiming the doors trapped them inside.

    Night suburban street with a tree, orange glow in the distance (no flames on people), memorial flowers; a lawsuit document with CLAIM tag; police report card 'SPEED + IMPAIRMENT'.

    LAWSUITS: CLAIMS, NOT RULINGS

    ANIMATIONGlow pulses; flowers; claim tag stamps.

  4. 4.04MED15.1s

    Regulators have opened investigations into Tesla door handles, and US lawmakers are pushing for a rule that every car must have a mechanical door release anyone can find. Tesla's design chief says it's working on combining the two.

    Capitol-style hearing room, a big red lever on a podium labelled 'MECHANICAL RELEASE'; a stylised designer nods and sketches a door with both a button and a pull handle.

    NHTSA PROBES · BILL IN CONGRESS

    ANIMATIONLever pulls with a clunk; sketch draws itself.

  5. 4.05MED10.6s

    That's the problem with treating a car like a phone. When a phone crashes, you restart it. When a car crashes, you need to get out.

    Split: a frozen phone with a spinning wheel; a crashed car with the door handle glowing; nodding dog shakes its head slowly.

    ANIMATIONSpinner spins; door handle glows; slow head shake.

The fightback

0:47 · 4 shots · 116 words
  1. 5.01WIDE8.7s

    So is there a way back? Volkswagen has already promised the buttons are returning. And Porsche just went one step further.

    Design studio: a box of chunky buttons carried back in on a trolley; a workshop door rolls up revealing a covered sports car.

    ANIMATIONTrolley rolls in; workshop door rises.

  2. 5.02MED15.1s

    And what did Porsche show next? The Mission S concept. A mid-engined supercar with a real key, real buttons, round dials with a proper needle, and no central screen. Need sat nav? There's a holder for your phone.

    A warm workshop; dust sheet off a low red concept; close-up: key turned, chunky toggles, an analogue rev needle sweeps; a phone clicks into a little holder; nodding dog nods wildly.

    PORSCHE MISSION S (CONCEPT)

    ANIMATIONKey turn, needle sweep, phone snaps into holder.

  3. 5.03MED12.4s

    So maybe there's hope. Let carmakers build phones on wheels if they want. But we already have phones. When buyers stop paying for them, watch how fast the buttons come back.

    Back on the M62, rain easing to golden dusk; Dave in a car with buttons presses demist by feel; nodding dog nods; EYES OFF ROAD meter resets to 0.

    EYES OFF ROAD: 0 m

    ANIMATIONSun breaks through; meter resets; dog nods.

  4. 5.04MED10.6s

    Would you trust a car that works like a phone? Tell me in the comments. And for more stories like this, subscribe to Stormi Explain Everything.

    End card space: Stormi mascot beside the nodding dog, comment bubble icon and subscribe button; clean area for end screen.

    ANIMATIONComment bubble pops; subscribe bell rings.

Fact log

Fixes against the transcript

  • Key Largo (Benavides v. Tesla): Apr 2019 Model S on Autopilot, driver George McGee reached for dropped phone, ran T-junction >60 mph, hit parked SUV; Naibel Benavides Leon (22) killed, Dillon Angulo injured. Aug 2025 Miami federal jury: Tesla 33% liable, ~$243M incl. $200M punitive; Judge Bloom upheld Feb 2026; Tesla appealing. (NPR, Fortune, Engadget)
  • NHTSA closed ~3-yr probe Apr 2024: 956 crashes reviewed, weak driver engagement, 13 fatal crashes. Dec 2023 recall 2M+ vehicles via OTA. (NPR, CBS)
  • California DMV adopted ALJ ruling Dec 2025 that Autopilot/FSD marketing misleading; Feb 2026 no suspension as Tesla stopped using 'Autopilot' in CA; Autopilot discontinued in US/Canada Jan 2026. (CA DMV, TechCrunch)
  • NHTSA FSD probe upgraded to engineering analysis Mar 2026, ~3.2M vehicles; reports of red-light running/wrong lane.
  • Feb 2021 recall ~135,000 Model S/X: 8GB eMMC wear -> loss of defrost/defog, rear camera. (CNBC, Engadget)
  • Bloomberg (2025): at least 15 deaths where occupants couldn't open Tesla doors after crash. NHTSA Model Y door probe Sept 2025, Model 3 Dec 2025. Tesla design chief: combining manual and electronic release.
  • Piedmont Cybertruck crash Nov 2024: 3 students died; CHP blamed speed and impairment; families' lawsuits CLAIM doors trapped them (not ruled).
  • Vi Bilägare 2022: 2005 Volvo V70 10 s/306 m; MG Marvel R 44.9 s. VW Mindt 'never, ever' (Mar 2025). Porsche Mission S concept: key, buttons, analogue tach, phone holder.
  • UK hand-held phone penalty: 6 points + £200.
  • No gore: crashes shown at distance as flashes/lights; victims not depicted; memorial only.
